definition: Harbinger means a sign that something is coming.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word harbinger. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know harbinger should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: In the orchard, the first windfall apples are a harbinger of the wasps that will own the rows by September.
A hint is the faintest rung — a trace you could miss or explain away, far milder than a harbinger.
A guarantee goes further than a harbinger: a harbinger announces that something is likely on its way, while a guarantee promises it cannot fail to arrive.

A herald announces what approaches, and the word keeps a whiff of the royal messenger sent ahead on purpose. A harbinger merely appears — first frost, first falling leaf — and the announcing lies in our reading of it. Heralds are sent; harbingers just show up.

An omen is a sign read for fate, good or ill — it belongs to superstition, and someone must interpret it. A harbinger is the practical early sign of something reliably on its way: no fate, no reading, just the arrival that announces the rest.

A bellwether is the lead member of the crowd itself — the first sheep through the gate, the county whose vote tracks the nation's. It belongs to what it predicts. A harbinger stands apart from what it announces, arriving ahead of an event it is no part of.

Forecasters on the Gulf coast keep an unglamorous instrument list, and the humblest entry is a swell gauge bolted to a buoy ninety miles offshore.
Days before a storm's clouds are visible, its energy arrives ahead of it as long, low swells that lift the buoy in a slow rhythm.
Veteran forecasters call that rhythm the storm's harbinger: it is not part of the storm, no one sends it as a message, and it needs no interpreting.
It is simply the thing that reliably arrives first, and the coast has learned to act on it -- boats in, shutters up.
Tourists sometimes read the calm, glassy weather between swells as a good sign.
